tagline: A rough desert climb reaches the Smithsonian’s former solar observatory
intro: Harquahala Mountain Back Country Byway climbs north from Eagle Eye Road for 10.5 miles to the summit. BLM describes a rugged, challenging road through Sonoran Desert scenery, with ecosystems changing as elevation increases. Its backcountry byway reaches the highest point in southwest Arizona, where BLM highlights views in every direction. The climb requires high clearance and four-wheel drive, and BLM recommends traveling it from November through April.

The summit served the U.S. Army as a heliograph station in the 1880s, before it became a place to study the sun. The Smithsonian built its observatory in 1920 to measure solar activity. The site was chosen for its remoteness from pollution and its high percentage of cloudless days. In 1925, the operation moved to Table Mountain, California, for easier access and better atmospheric conditions. The original Arizona observatory is a two-story adobe structure covered with corrugated tin, supported by wooden beams.

On the ascent from Eagle Eye Road, old mining debris, shafts and stone houses mark earlier mining activity. The drive ends at the observatory on the summit; its building has been stabilized since entering the National Register in 1975. A pack trail continues down the mountain through the wilderness, with steep and difficult sections.

moments.title: Old mining ground
moments.text: Mining remains appear along the climb: debris, shafts and stone houses left by earlier miners. They lie along a road BLM describes as rugged and challenging for off-highway vehicles. The Sonoran Desert setting changes with elevation, and flowering plants bloom from March through May.
moments.notice: Old mining debris, shafts and stone houses appear along the drive.

moments.title: Harquahala Peak Observatory
moments.text: Corrugated tin covers a two-story adobe observatory at the summit, with a wooden porch on the second story. The Smithsonian built it in 1920 to measure and record solar activity. Observers worked here until 1925, when the operation moved to Table Mountain, California, seeking easier access and better atmospheric conditions. The Arizona building was listed on the National Register in 1975 and has since been stabilized. A cement water-catchment device sits at its northern end. Below the building are semi-arid plains at elevations of 1,500 to 2,000 feet.

moments.title: Summit pack trail
moments.text: The pack trail leaves the summit and descends through the Harquahala Wilderness, with several steep and difficult portions. The wilderness was designated in 1990 and lies north and east of the summit. BLM identifies the descending route as a hike.

practical: Old mining ground: High clearance and four-wheel drive are required. No drinking water is available. BLM recommends November through April for this road. (checked 2026-10-11)

sources.label: Bureau of Land Management, Harquahala Mountain Back Country Byway
